title: Love close

lines: A LADDER. A ROAD. A TOWEL.
cards: A philosopher's ladder. A myth about humans split in two. A widow on a dusty road, refusing to turn back.
A basin of water and a towel. A mother guarding her only child. A coat by the door that nobody can bring themselves to move.
This block of sixty days opened with a handful of words for love and a question: one thing, or many? Before the hills turn to something new, look back once. Today: Diotima.

teach.b: First, the philosophers. In Plato's Symposium, Diotima teaches that love climbs, from one beautiful person toward beauty itself. Aristotle calls a friend another self.
Montaigne, asked why he loved his friend, could only say: because it was he, because it was I.
Second, the scriptures. Ruth, to her mother-in-law Naomi: “whither thou goest, I will go.” Jesus kneels and washes his friends' feet.
A letter of John puts it in three words: “God is love.” In the Qur'an, one of God's names is the Loving.
Third, the small. Thérèse of Lisieux and her little way: the smallest actions, done for love. The Dhammapada's water-pot, filled drop by drop.
The letter of James: “swift to hear, slow to speak.” Simone Weil, holding that attention is a rare and pure kind of generosity. Fourth, the turn these sixty days kept making.

Again and again, the texts treated love less as a feeling that happens to you and more as something done: keeping a friendship from fading, listening without fixing, letting a grown child go, sitting with grief, writing the note.

The traditions disagree about a great deal, and their loves stay different, as yesterday showed. But the texts kept coming back to hands and feet: a towel, a road, a cup of water, a word said out loud.
Love, in these sixty days, has mostly been a verb.

how: Traditions keep love through practice: Christians through service and prayer, Buddhists through loving-kindness meditation and small daily good deeds, and friends and families by saying it out loud.

games.q: sixty days on love are ending, and you want to keep one thing from them. what do the lessons point to?
o: wait until the feeling is strong enough.
find the single right word for love.
games.why: from a towel and basin to a note on paper, the texts kept treating love as something done.

practice: Bring to mind one person who hasn't heard it from you lately, maybe someone you'd never think to tell, and let their face come clear.
Let the words form as plainly as you'd say them: I love you, or, if that isn't how your family talks, the version that is, like thanks for being you, or I think about you.
If you pray, you can hold them in your own tradition's words.

wordCard.voice: Diotima, the philosopher in Plato's Symposium who teaches that love climbs from one beautiful person toward beauty itself. Sixty days on love, from her philosopher's ladder to a note on paper, ending where it kept landing: in what we do. Today's word.
